title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). Two preregistered design choices—shared_initial_generation (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions) and reuse of the same deterministic validator as both the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer—produced a deterministic ceiling effect in this run that rendered the primary estimand uninformative for assessing generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics. The preregistered design (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt‑5‑mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime guard and scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes) and shared_initial_generation semantics. Confirmatory outcomes (archived artifacts) show complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). We present the preregistered methodology, exact artifact‑grounded results, an artifact‑grounded diagnosis explaining why the design choices produced a ceiling, an aggregated difficulty summary computed from the archived task manifest, and concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being applied to translate operator intent into network configuration artifacts and staged change workflows (canaries, progressive rollout, rollback). Prior work shows LLMs can synthesize syntactically plausible configuration templates in testbeds and benchmarks, while verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair workflows and deterministic network verifiers reduce syntactic and semantic IaC errors. The operational question is end‑to‑end: how do generator variability, runtime verification, staged rollout semantics, repair, and rollback interact to affect safe‑deploy outcomes?

Research question. Under the preregistered ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1 semantics, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) measured on N=400 paired tasks.

Contributions and high‑level finding. We (1) present a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; (2) report exact, archive‑verifiable confirmatory results that show universal acceptance of shared generator outputs by the deterministic validator (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0); and (3) provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis demonstrating that preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics together with reuse of the same deterministic validator produced a deterministic ceiling that makes the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard interaction in this execution. From archived traces we derive concrete, implementable benchmark‑hardening recommendations for future preregistered runs.
sections.related_work:
This study combines prior lines of work: (i) intent→configuration generation using LLMs, (ii) verifier‑guided generate–validate‑repair pipelines in IaC and provisioning contexts, (iii) deterministic network verification and reachability tools, and (iv) agentic/tool‑augmented LLM architectures for AIOps.

Intent→configuration: recent demonstrations show LLMs can translate operator intent into configuration templates in controlled settings (e.g., intent‑based network configuration studies and PreConfig). These works evaluate generation quality and utility but typically do not measure staged‑rollout safety or closed‑loop blocking.

Verifier‑guided IaC: verifier‑guided loops and verifier‑led fine‑tuning (e.g., TerraFormer) report correctness gains in IaC and provisioning contexts; these motivate runtime verifier integration but do not demonstrate production‑scale closed‑loop runtime blocking with staged rollouts.

Deterministic verification: header‑space and reachability tools, and Kubernetes reachability analyses, are effective at finding configuration errors in emulated/offline settings but differ in modeling assumptions and scope.

Agentic LLMs for AIOps: multi‑agent and tool‑augmented pipelines expand capability but introduce failure modes (hallucination, misapplied tools, miscalibrated confidence) that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployments. Surveys repeatedly note an evaluation gap: community‑standard, action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollouts, repair, rollback, and provenance are limited. Our experiment operationalizes a compact action‑aware staging benchmark under a strict preregistered design to surface concrete design pitfalls and practical mitigations.

(Verified nearby works used for positioning are listed in the References.)
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. We preregistered the study as cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1. The primary confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (two‑sided, α=0.05). The preregistered analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) runs a permutation‑based paired difference test and reports exact permutation p‑values; an exact McNemar two‑sided test is reported for corroboration. Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) were frozen for secondary outcomes.

Adapter semantics, shared generation, and the explicit ceiling consequence. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer. Critically, preregistration set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): each task produced a single deterministic LLM generation that was delivered identically to both baseline and guarded episodes. Because the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation, when the validator accepts a shared candidate both episodes necessarily record safe‑deploy outcomes. We therefore explicitly state here (and mirror in the Abstract) that these preregistered choices render the primary estimand uninformative for assessing generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics in this execution.

Episode flow and repair rules. For each task the adapter requested a single shared candidate from gpt‑5‑mini, delivered that candidate to both episodes, and (in the guarded episode) routed the candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which applied full intent‑constraint validation using a deterministic rule set recorded in validator_trace entries. The preregistered repair policy permitted up to one repair attempt in the guarded episode. All repair invocations, repair_applied flags, validation_before/after states, and final validity decisions were recorded in the archived validator traces; in this run repair_applied = false for all episodes.

Task generation and deterministic replay. Tasks were generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each task includes structured difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, pattern, required_command_count, and level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). The preregistration required deterministic three‑replay consistency checks per agent+simulator pair; pairs failing replay or encountering simulator errors would be flagged and excluded per the missingness_plan. In this run all three‑replay checks passed and no exclusions were applied.

Analysis plan. The primary analysis uses exact permutation on paired safe‑deploy booleans (α=0.05); exact McNemar corroborates permutation results. Secondary outcomes include bootstrap CIs for median time‑to‑rollback and counts of repair attempts. Sensitivity analyses (treat excluded pairs as failures; restricted permutation) were preregistered but not needed because there were no exclusions. All analysis code, seeds, and logs are archived.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and reconciliation. The run started 2026‑08‑29T18:23:37Z and completed 2026‑08‑29T19:12:38Z. Planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 400 (shared initial generation); complete_pairs = 400. Deterministic three‑replay checks passed for all pairs; no exclusions were recorded.

Primary confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑grounded). Primary contingency counts: baseline_success_count = 400 (baseline_success_rate = 1.0); guarded_success_count = 400 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n_11 = 400 with n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0, yielding observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. The preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Cohen's h = 0.0. These results are reproduced directly from archived analysis artifacts (analysis/*).

Repair and rollback observations. Across 800 episodes repair_applied = false and no rollbacks were invoked; validator_trace entries show validation_after.final_state matched expected_final_state for accepted configurations. This explains universal acceptance: when the shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5, both episodes necessarily recorded safe‑deploy outcomes.

Aggregated difficulty summary (artifact‑derived). We computed per‑task difficulty counts by aggregating the archived execution/task_manifest.jsonl difficulty labels. The benchmark composition across the N=400 tasks was: medium = 120 tasks (30.0%), hard = 140 tasks (35.0%), very_hard = 140 tasks (35.0%). These aggregated counts are produced from the archived manifest and are included to support the manuscript claim of benchmark heterogeneity; per‑task difficulty labels and the manifest are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl for auditor verification.

Representative worked example. A compact representative pair (archived): task-000001 required migrating edge1 to VLAN 30 and MTU 1600 with a safe shutdown→change→restore sequence. The shared candidate and both condition responses are identical in the archive; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 validated the candidate (validation_after.valid = true) so both episodes recorded score = 1. An excerpt of the validator_trace for task-000001 is archived among execution/scoring/*.json and illustrated in the artifact examples.

Statistical interpretation. The observed ceiling collapses inferential variance: permutation and McNemar tests correctly report p = 1.0, but those statistics do not provide evidence about generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics because the design prevented the guard from having an opportunity to intervene. The preregistered power calculation assumed non‑ceiling baseline rates and within‑pair variability sufficient to detect ≈0.10 absolute differences with N=400; those assumptions are invalidated by the observed deterministic ceiling and therefore the original power rationale does not apply to these results.
sections.discussion:
Why the primary estimand became uninformative. Two preregistered design choices produced the deterministic ceiling. First, shared_initial_generation intentionally removed generator variance by delivering identical LLM outputs to baseline and guarded episodes. Second, the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When the deterministic validator accepts the shared candidate, both conditions record identical safe‑deploy outcomes and the paired difference must be zero. This is a construct‑validity outcome of the frozen design, not a general null statement about verifier utility across diverse generator/validator pairings.

Consequences for power, inference, and interpretation. The preregistered power calculation relied on within‑pair variability that did not occur in this run. The observed ceiling thus invalidates the power rationale and collapses inferential uncertainty: exact p‑values of 1.0 correctly reflect the data but cannot adjudicate whether a runtime guard would have improved outcomes under an alternative design that preserved generator variance.

Artifact‑grounded benchmark hardening recommendations. Using archived validator_trace and execution accounting we recommend concrete implementation steps for future preregistered runs that preserve signal for generator×guard interactions and that are directly implementable from the existing artifact bundle:

1) Independent per‑condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true) so each condition receives independently sampled generator outputs and the guard has bona fide opportunities to accept, block, or request repair.

2) Distinct runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer implementations (or a held‑out scorer) to prevent conflation of runtime acceptance and analysis scoring; validator_trace acceptance fields and separate scorer outputs should be compared only when implementations differ.

3) Controlled adversarial seeding: preregister a reproducible fraction of perturbation seeds guaranteed to produce nontrivial baseline failure rates to preserve power (the deterministic task generator supports seeded perturbations recorded in the manifest).

4) Difficulty‑stratified sampling: ensure a sufficient proportion of very_hard tasks to produce measurable baseline errors; the per‑task difficulty labels in execution/task_manifest.jsonl enable deterministic stratified draws.

5) Instrumented mitigation metrics: record repair attempts, repairs applied, and time‑to‑rollback as preregistered secondary outcomes (these fields exist in validator_trace and repair logs in the artifact bundle).

Operational implications. For NetOps practitioners: (i) experiment designs that remove generation variance can mask the benefits of runtime guards; and (ii) independent adjudication channels (distinct scorers or human reviewers) are important for measuring guard impact. Benchmarks evaluating runtime safety mechanisms should preserve signal for guard interventions through independent generation, adversarial perturbations, or heterogeneous validators.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling effect resulted from frozen design and implementation homogeneity and renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to support hardened follow‑on experiments (independent generation, adversarial seeding, heterogeneous validators) that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors. The artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations supplied here offer concrete steps researchers can preregister to preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility in NetOps settings.

Reproducibility note. All execution and analysis artifacts supporting the reported numbers and traces are archived in the bundled artifact set (execution/* and analysis/*). Key artifacts include the execution manifest, raw results, model configuration, deterministic validator traces, the task manifest with per‑task difficulty metadata, and the analysis results (paired contingency and bootstrap outputs). Auditors can reproduce the reported summaries using the archived manifests and analysis code as recorded in the artifact bundle.

Final interpretive boundary. The null paired difference observed here is a valid, artifact‑grounded outcome for the preregistered design but should not be interpreted as evidence that runtime verification is unnecessary in general. Instead, it illustrates how specific preregistered design choices (shared generation and reuse of the same deterministic validator for runtime and scoring) can eliminate the statistical signal needed to evaluate generator×guard closed‑loop effects. Evaluations that wish to measure guard utility must preserve generator variance and independent adjudication as described above.

limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and can be audited; this manuscript reports artifact‑derived aggregated counts (Table 2) rather than fabricating counts from unsupported summaries.
